other_side: Zitron's Manifesto reads a list like Lieberman's thirty features as the disease, not the cure. Building a harness, keeping context files, distributing skills and throwing the whole thing away every three months is what Robin Sloan calls 'Jarvising': tinkering with your assistant until the tinkering becomes the work, producing 'the sense that you're being really, really productive' without anything measurable coming out the other end. He argues enterprises moved onto token-based billing this year and promptly started cutting budgets, because costs rose exponentially while nobody could point to an improvement beyond people saying they felt productive. And he says the constant rebuilding NLW celebrates is not a discipline but a symptom: nothing yet works as a stable product, so customers must keep re-plumbing whenever a model, price or harness changes.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether an organisation's AI spend produces output that survives an audit. Both accept as fact that agentic tooling has spread fast in 2026, that costs are volatile and now metered per token, and that companies rebuild their workflows often. The empirical question that will resolve is whether firms that adopt the 'AI-native' pattern show measurable gains, and the observable is dull: token budgets in enterprise renewals over the next two quarters, and whether 'cost per accepted pull request' or a similar metric appears in public company disclosures. The residue is worldview: NLW sees churn as learning, Zitron sees it as churn. For NLW to be vindicated, the throw-it-away-quarterly cadence must produce rising output per pound; for Zitron, budgets must be cut once the feeling fades. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype, and they agree on one thing: today's measurement is poor. Watch renewal-season token budgets.
